title: Geometric properties preserved by representable Weil restriction
statement: Let $p:S'\to S$ be a finite locally free morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-pc-finite-locally-free], and let $Z\to S'$ be a scheme. Suppose an $S$-scheme $W$ represents $X\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{S'}(X\times_SS',Z)$ by natural bijections [def-pc-fibre-product]. Each of the following implications holds independently: if $Z\to S'$ is separated, then $W\to S$ is separated; if it is locally of finite type, then $W\to S$ is locally of finite type; if it is smooth, then $W\to S$ is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Separated means the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. If $S$ is locally Noetherian [pqf-def-locnoeth] and $Z\to S'$ is quasi-compact, then $W\to S$ is quasi-compact. Quasi-compact means the inverse image of each affine open in the target has a finite subcover from any open cover.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5, printed pp.195–198 (PDF pp.201–204), properties (a),(b),(c),(h): (a) with locally Noetherian base, the other three without additional hypotheses. Local PDF WANTED; primary-source scan read at https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~kamenova/homepage_files/Bosch_Raynaud_Neron_Model_tc.pdf.

proof.text: The representing bijections give an evaluation $W\times_SS'\to Z$. For every $B\to S$, their restriction to $B$-schemes identifies $W\times_SB$ with the restriction of $Z\times_SB$ along $S'\times_SB\to B$: both sides assign to $T/B$ the same set $\operatorname{Hom}_{S'}(T\times_SS',Z)$. Likewise maps to a fibre product correspond to pairs with equal composites, so restriction preserves fibre products and diagonals. These are identities of the specified functors, not extra representability assumptions. We may work over affine opens of $S$ on which $p$ has constant rank and its section algebra has a finite basis; the rank and basis results cited apply without a Noetherian hypothesis.

source.place: BLR 7.6 after Lemma 1 and Proposition 5: base change, fibre products; Stacks Tags 04MH and 02K9 for affine basis charts

proof.text: Assume $Z/S'$ separated. Set $B=W\times_SW$, $E=B\times_SS'$, and let $D\hookrightarrow E$ be the equalizer of the two evaluation maps to $Z$, i.e. the pullback of $\Delta_{Z/S'}$. It is closed: on affine charts a pullback of a quotient ring map $A\to A/I$ is $A'\to A'/IA'$, still surjective. By the degree theorem $B=\coprod_dB_d$ with $B_d$ open and closed and $E_d=E\times_BB_d\to B_d$ finite locally free of degree $d$. Apply the containment-locus theorem to $f=p_B:E\to B$ and the $B$-scheme $T=B_d$ (so $X_T=E_d$), taking as its finite locally free closed subscheme all of $E_d\subseteq X_T$ (degree $d$ over $B_d$) and as its closed immersion $D\cap E_d\hookrightarrow E_d$ (letters of the theorem renamed to avoid the $Z,W$ of the item): it gives a closed $C_d\hookrightarrow B_d$, and $C=\coprod_dC_d$ is closed in $B$. A $B$-scheme $T$ splits as $\coprod_dT\times_BB_d$, so $T\to B$ factors through $C$ exactly when $E_T\to E$ factors through $D$, i.e. when the two evaluation maps on $E_T$ agree; the representing bijections say exactly that the two maps $T\to W$ agree. Thus $C\hookrightarrow B$ represents the diagonal $W\to W\times_SW$, which is therefore a closed immersion, proving separatedness.

Work over $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $S'=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with a basis of rank $d$. For any affine $S'$-scheme $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ choose a $B$-presentation of $C$. The existing affine-chart node supplies an affine restriction $H_U$. The coefficient-algebra node gives its coordinate algebra $D$: its natural bijection on affine tests identifies $\operatorname{Spec}D$ with $H_U$, and these identifications extend to scheme tests by gluing morphisms on affine covers. If $C$ has finitely many algebra generators, choose $I$ finite: $D$ is a quotient of a polynomial algebra on $d|I|$ variables, so is finitely generated, without any finiteness requirement on the relation ideal. If $C$ is finitely presented, choose both $I,K$ finite: $D$ has $d|I|$ generators and at most $d|K|$ specified relations, hence is finitely presented. These deductions are exactly the definitions of finite generation and presentation.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(c),(d), affine case; Stacks 05Y6 coefficient equations

proof.text: Let $(U_i)$ be an affine open cover of $Z$, and form $A=\coprod_iU_i\to Z$. This map is etale and surjective: on each open summand it is an open immersion. For each finite subset $J$ of indices put $A_J=\coprod_{i\in J}U_i$, an affine scheme. The preceding step gives an affine restriction $H_J$. Its map to $W$ is etale: over a scheme $T\to W$ its fibre is the section space of the etale map $(T\times_SS')\times_Z A_J\to T\times_SS'$, so the etale-section-space theorem applies to the finite locally free family $T\times_SS'\to T$. The family $(H_J\to W)_J$ is jointly surjective. Indeed apply the local-section theorem to $A\times_Z(W\times_SS')\to W\times_SS'$ to obtain an etale surjection $V\to W$ and a lift $V\times_SS'\to A$. Restrict $V$ to affine opens. Its finite preimage is affine and quasi-compact, so the disjoint open summands of $A$ meet its image in only finitely many indices. The lift therefore factors through some $A_J$, yielding $V\to H_J\to W$. Thus the images of the $H_J$ cover $W$.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(c),(d), affine reduction made precise by Stacks 05XR and 05XQ

proof.text: Suppose $Z\to S'$ is locally of finite type. Choose the affine opens $U_i$ in step 4 with finitely generated $B$-algebras of sections. Each finite union $A_J$ has coordinate ring a finite product of these algebras. This product is finitely generated over $B$: adjoin the finitely many coordinate idempotents and the finitely many generators in their respective factors. Step 3 makes $H_J\to S$ locally of finite type. Since the $H_J\to W$ are a jointly surjective etale family, they are flat and locally finitely presented, and local finite type descends along their coproduct by the cited source-descent theorem. Hence $W\to S$ is locally of finite type. No separatedness, quasi-compactness, or Noetherian assumption was used.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(c); Stacks 02KL (local finite type through flat lfp surjective source maps)

proof.text: For later use the same affine atlas also proves that $W/S$ is locally of finite presentation whenever $Z/S'$ is. For each $U_i$, the affine-opens theorem makes its coordinate algebra finitely presented over $B$. Their finite coproduct $A_J/S'$ is locally finitely presented by the finite-coproduct theorem, and, being affine over the affine $S'$, its coordinate algebra is finitely presented by the affine-opens theorem again. The finite-variable finite-relation calculation in step 3 makes each $H_J/S$ locally finitely presented. Apply local finite presentation's fppf-source locality to the jointly surjective etale atlas in step 4.

Suppose $Z/S'$ is smooth. It is locally finitely presented, so step 6 gives local finite presentation of $W/S$. Given an affine first-order thickening $T_0\hookrightarrow T$ over $S$ and $T_0\to W$, the representing bijection gives $T_0\times_SS'\to Z$. The schemes $T\times_SS'$ and $T_0\times_SS'$ are affine because they are finite over affine schemes. The induced immersion is first order: locally it is the quotient by $IB$ for a square-zero ideal $I$, and $(IB)^2=0$. Formal smoothness of $Z/S'$ supplies a lift $T\times_SS'\to Z$. The representing bijection gives the required lift $T\to W$, whose restriction is the original map by naturality. Thus $W/S$ is formally smooth and locally finitely presented, hence smooth in the cited definition.

We now prove quasi-compactness only. The following radicial case will also be used for an intermediate base: let $p:E\to B$ be finite locally free and a universal homeomorphism, and let $Y/E$ be quasi-compact. The restriction $R$ exists as an algebraic space by the cited existence theorem. Over an affine basis chart of $B$, $E$ is affine and $Y$ has a finite affine open cover $(U_i)$. Each $R(U_i)$ is affine by step 3 (no finiteness condition on its equations). It is an open subspace of $R$: over any test $T\to R$, the condition that the evaluation on $E_T$ lies in $U_i$ is exactly the open containment locus. These finitely many open subspaces cover $R$. Indeed a point can be tested after a field extension, and $E\times_B\operatorname{Spec}K$ has exactly one underlying point; its map to $Y$ factors through an affine open containing its image. Thus $R$ has a finite affine etale cover on every affine basis chart of $B$. For an arbitrary affine scheme $V\to B$, the base change $E_V\to V$ is again finite locally free and a universal homeomorphism, $Y_V/E_V$ is quasi-compact, and $R\times_BV$ is the restriction of $Y_V$ along $E_V\to V$ (step 1); $V$ is covered by finitely many affine basis charts, so $R\times_BV$ is covered by finitely many open subspaces with finite affine etale covers and is quasi-compact. By the affine-test theorem $R\to B$ is quasi-compact. This argument also applies to $B$ empty.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(a), radicial case; Stacks 05YF for intermediate space existence

proof.text: If $E\to B$ is finite etale and $Y\to E$ is quasi-compact (a scheme or one of the open-affine-covered spaces just constructed), its restriction is quasi-compact. Restrict to affine constant-degree pieces of $B$ and trivialize the finite etale morphism etale-locally by the cited splitting theorem. Over each trivializing scheme $V$, the restriction is the finite fibre product over $V$ of the pullbacks $Y_i$ to the copies of $V$. Quasi-compactness of each $Y_i\to V$ follows from base-change stability. Over an affine open in $V$, choose finite affine charts of each $Y_i$; products of those charts over this affine base are affine, and finitely many suffice to cover the product. Thus the product is quasi-compact. To descend, for each affine open in $B$ take finitely many affine opens of the etale trivializing family whose open images cover it, and form their finite coproduct $V_0$. Then $V_0\to B$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact (source quasi-compact and target affine), so fpqc quasi-compactness descent applies when the restriction is a scheme, in particular to the given $W$. The empty product is $V$ and is quasi-compact over itself.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(a), finite etale case and products

proof.text: Assume $S$ locally Noetherian and $Z/S'$ quasi-compact. Work over an affine open $S_0=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A$ Noetherian, from a covering of $S$ as in the definition of locally Noetherian; its underlying space is Noetherian, and every closed subscheme of $S_0$ is the spectrum of a Noetherian quotient of $A$. On each integral reduced closed subscheme $C\subseteq S$, work affine-locally and apply the generic-factorization node to $S'\times_SC\to C$. On a nonempty open $U\subseteq C$ this gives $S'_U\xrightarrow{u}T\xrightarrow{e}U$, with $u$ finite locally free and a universal homeomorphism, and $e$ finite etale. First restrict $Z_U$ along $u$, obtaining the quasi-compact algebraic space of step 8. Restrict that space along $e$. On functors this composite is the original restriction, since for every $A/U$ the evaluation on $A\times_UT$ of the first restriction is $\operatorname{Hom}_{S'_U}(A\times_US'_U,Z_U)$. Thus its representing space is $W_U$, which is a scheme by the hypothesis and base change in step 1. Step 9 applies to $W_U$ and makes it quasi-compact over $U$. The rank-zero case is included: the restriction of the empty family is $U$.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(a), generic etale/radicial factorization and transitivity

proof.text: Finish by Noetherian induction on closed subsets $C$ of the affine base. Give each $C$ its reduced scheme structure; this does not change the space of $W_C$, since base change of a quotient by a nil ideal is again a quotient by a nil ideal. The empty subset is the base case. A Noetherian closed set has finitely many irreducible components; discard their pairwise intersections and choose a nonempty affine open in each remaining integral component to which step 10 applies. Their union $U\subseteq C$ is open, meets every generic point, and $W_U$ is a finite union of quasi-compact spaces after choosing quasi-compact opens as supplied there. The complement $C\setminus U$ is a proper closed subset, so the induction hypothesis makes $W_{C\setminus U}$ quasi-compact. Its underlying space together with $|W_U|$ covers $|W_C|$. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact: restrict any open cover to each and take the union of the finite subcovers. This proves quasi-compactness of $W_C$. For $C=S_0$ the scheme $W_{S_0}$ is quasi-compact and $S_0$ is affine, hence quasi-separated, so $W_{S_0}\to S_0$ is quasi-compact by the permanence theorem. These $S_0$ cover $S$, so $W\to S$ is quasi-compact by the open-covering criterion of the affine-test theorem, which for this representable morphism is quasi-compactness in the scheme sense.

source.place: BLR 7.6 Proposition 5(a), final Noetherian induction; elementary finite-union argument

lean.statement: theorem weilRestriction_geometric_properties {S S' Z W : Scheme.{u}} (p : S' ⟶ S) [p.IsFiniteLocallyFree] (z : Z ⟶ S') (w : W ⟶ S) (hrep : Nonempty (yoneda.obj (Over.mk w) ≅ (Over.pullback p).op ⋙ yoneda.obj (Over.mk z))) : (IsSeparated z → IsSeparated w) ∧ (LocallyOfFiniteType z → LocallyOfFiniteType w) ∧ (Smooth z → Smooth w) ∧ (IsLocallyNoetherian S → QuasiCompact z → QuasiCompact w)
